messages.content:
RoadDraft is a headless 2D CAD engine for roadway plans. Model space is US survey feet, and a point is [x, y] = [easting, northing] -- the other way round from how coordinates are usually spoken, so N 5000, E 2000 is [2000, 5000]. Sheets are paper inches seen through viewports at a feet-per-inch scale. Work through the commands: each one validates its params and explains what was wrong, every change is journaled and undoable. Start with get_document_state to see what is in the document, list_commands for the full surface, and render_sheet or render_model to look at your work.

To annotate something, find it before you point at it. In a sheet file the design usually lives in a referenced basefile, so the document owns no geometry of its own; find_entities searches the attachments too. Filter by what a thing IS -- layer, type, or its design anchor -- rather than dumping the document: find_entities {anchor: {kind: 'offset', offset: [-12, 12]}, visible_on: 'C-102'} is the pavement edges that sheet shows. Then pass the id straight to place_callout as target_entity, and the engine puts the leader tip on the geometry. Do not compute the point yourself: the midpoint of a curve's endpoints is not on the curve, and roadway linework runs parallel a few feet apart, so a hand-computed point usually lands on the wrong line rather than on nothing. If you do pass a raw target point, read the warning that comes back -- it names what the tip actually touched.

Some things are not entities at all -- a station, a PC, a point at an offset. Ask the design for those: list_alignments with include_references=true names a referenced alignment 'DESIGN:SR-100', and station_to_xy, xy_to_station, resolve_anchor and get_design_data all accept that name and answer in host coordinates. To call one out, give place_callout a target_anchor ('18+00@12R', 'PC-1') and that alignment name. Otherwise commands do not take it: nothing can be drawn, labelled or anchored to an alignment this document does not own.

Plan annotation belongs on the sheet, in paper inches, not in the model. Pass the sheet as place_callout's space and still name a model target -- target_entity or target_anchor: the engine sees it through the sheet's viewport (scale and twist included) and puts the tip where it shows on the paper. 'at' then runs along the part of the entity that sheet shows, since a pavement edge runs the whole project and a sheet shows one stretch. find_entities with visible_on gives each row a sheet_point, which is where that tip will land -- use it to choose a position for the text that is clear of the linework. Never work out a viewport by hand: model_to_sheet and sheet_to_model convert, and station_to_xy and point_on_entity take a sheet and answer in paper inches as well.

Do one drafting task in a headless CAD engine called RoadDraft, using the tools you have been given. They are your ENTIRE tool surface.

Rules:
- Every change to the drawing must go through a tool call.
- The document is already open and saves itself after each command. Do not save it under another name.
- Nobody can answer questions. Work until you judge the task done, then stop and give your report.
- You have no calculator or code execution. Any arithmetic you need, do yourself.

THE TASK:
Create alignment RAMP-B. It begins at N 1000.00, E 1000.00, station 10+00, and runs N 62°30'00" E for 900.00 ft to a PI. There it deflects 35°00'00" to the right and continues 1,100.00 ft to its end. Use a 600 ft radius curve at the PI. Draw its centerline on layer V-ALIGN-CNTR.

When finished, reply briefly with:
1. What you created and drew (names, layers, key coordinates).
2. The tool calls that mattered, in order (tool name + the key arguments).
3. Anything that failed, confused you, or that you had to work around -- quote error messages. If you had to compute coordinates yourself, show the arithmetic.

messages.thinking:
We need to perform drafting steps:

- Create a layer V-ALIGN-CNTR if not existing.
- Create alignment RAMP-B with begin station 10+00 and PI coordinates etc.
We need to compute coordinates of the PI (end of first segment) given start N1000 E1000, bearing N62°30'00"E, distance 900 ft.

In bearing notation: N θ° E means from north toward east? Actually typical surveying: N θ° E means start from north, turn eastwards by θ. So azimuth from north clockwise: N62°30'E yields bearing az = 90-62.5? Wait standard: N θ° E is measured east of north. So azimuth from north is 62°30' towards east, i.e., bearing is 90-? Actually azimuth measured from north clockwise: NθE is same as bearing of θ east of north, so azimuth = θ. So angle from north to east direction is 90°, but you go east of north by 62.5°, so azimuth = 62.5° measured from north clockwise (i.e., 62.5° east of north). In typical coordinate (X east, Y north), delta X = distance * sin(az), delta Y = distance * cos(az). So compute sin(62.5°) and cos(62.5°). Need approximate values: sin62.5≈0.883, cos62.5≈0.469. Multiply by 900 ft:
ΔX = 900 * sin62.5 ≈ 900*0.883 = 794.7 ft.
ΔY = 900 * cos62.5 ≈ 900*0.469 = 422.1 ft.

Thus PI coordinate: start E=1000, N=1000. Add ΔX to easting (X) => 1000 + 794.7 ≈ 1794.7. Add ΔY to northing (Y) => 1000 + 422.1 ≈ 1422.1.

Now second segment: deflects 35° to the right. Right deflection means bearing turns to the right relative to travel direction. Starting bearing was N62.5E (az 62.5°). Right turn of 35° means new bearing az = 62.5° + 35° = 97.5°? Actually right turn means clockwise increase of bearing. So new bearing approx 97.5° from north. That is slightly east of south? Wait 90° is east, 97.5° is 7.5° south of east (i.e., E7.5°S). Represent as E7.5°S or S? But we can compute components: az = 62.5 + 35 = 97.5°. Sin(97.5) = sin(180-97.5?) Actually sin(97.5)= sin(82.5) but positive? sin >0. sin97.5≈0.991. cos97.5≈ -0.130 (since beyond 90). So ΔX = 1100 * sin97.5 ≈ 1100*0.991 = 1090.1. ΔY = 1100 * cos97.5 ≈ 1100*(-0.130) = -143 ft.

Thus end coordinate: E = 1794.7 + 1090.1 ≈ 2884.8. N = 1422.1 + (-143) ≈ 1279.1.

But we also need a curve of radius 600 ft at PI between tangent 1 and tangent 2. The curve deflection is 35°, radius 600. The length along curve = radius * deflection rad. deflection rad = 35° * π/180 = 0.6109 rad. Curve length = 600 * 0.6109 = 366.5 ft approx.

But we have segment distances: first tangent 900 ft to PI, then curve radius 600 ft, then second tangent length after curve? The problem says continue 1,100 ft to its end, using a 600 ft radius curve at the PI. Likely means after curve, continue along new tangent for 1,100 ft to end point (the arc is part of the path; total after PI includes curve + tangent). However typical alignment definition: you give a PI (point of intersection) and radius, then you need to compute PC and PT offset distances (point of curvature and point of tangency). For a simple alignment creation command, we can provide PI coordinates and radius maybe. But the create_alignment command expects a sequence of PIs with optional radius for interior points. The spec: create_alignment takes name, begin_station, pis: each Pi is [x, y] for begin/end, [x, y, R] interior. So we can provide three points: start point, a PI with radius (i.e., interior point with radius), and end point.

Thus we need to compute coordinates for point after curve? Actually for alignment we supply points along the alignment: the interior point with radius is the PI location. The engine will compute the curve geometry itself using radius and deflection angle. But we must provide the PI coordinates (which we computed). And the end point coordinate after second tangent length from PI, but note the alignment generation will treat interior point with radius causing a curve but will shift the endpoints because tangent lengths are from PC to PT not the full 900 and 1100? Wait typical alignment: you have start point, then along initial tangent length to PC (point of curvature), then curve of length L then PT then second tangent. To define using PI method, you supply start point, PI coordinate (including radius?), and end point; the engine uses the radius to compute the curve that just touches the tangents? Not sure. But the create_alignment command expects interior point list maybe as [x, y, R] where R is radius and the PI is given as coordinates of the point of intersection of the two tangents (i.e., where they would meet if not curved). That matches typical design: you give PI location, radius, and the engine computes PC and PT offset distances based on geometry. For that, we need to supply the PI coordinate, which we have.

Thus need to compute the end point coordinate given the second tangent length after PT? Actually if we give the end point coordinate after full tangent, the alignment generation may compute a curve that is placed such that PC is offset from PI, and PT also offset; the end point will be offset from the PI by distance equal to second tangent length + offset? Let’s think: The PI method: you have start point, PI, end point, radius. The engine creates a curve that is tangent to the lines from start to PI and from PI to end. The curve is placed such that its tangents meet the initial and final straight lines at points PC and PT respectively. The positions of PC and PT are determined by radius and deflection angle determined by geometry. The length of straight from start to PC is less than the straight distance from start to PI. Same for after curve to end. So we need to provide the start point and the end point as the actual endpoints of alignment (start and termination). The start point is given. The end point is not the coordinate we previously computed (since that's after full 1100 ft beyond PI). However we used a deflection of 35°, so the direction after curve is 35° right of initial direction, exactly as needed. The length from PI to end point should be 1100 ft after the curve—meaning the straight line from PI to end point is 1100 ft? Actually spec says "continues 1,100.00 ft to its end." That likely means the tangent length after curve is 1100 ft, measured along the new direction (post-deflection). So the endpoint is at PI plus 1100 ft along new bearing (which we computed as 2884.8,1279.1). However with curve, the PT will be some distance back from PI along the new direction; the end point will be further beyond PT by the remaining length 1100 - offset (?), but the spec may ignore offset details. Since we use create_alignment with PI and radius, the engine calculates PC/PT automatically, but we have to give end point coordinate that is down the new direction at the total distance 1100 from PI? Actually the true location of end point is after the entire new tangent length from PT. So we must compute the point at 1100 ft along the new bearing from PI, not from PT. But the alignment will then offset the PT back by offset distance R*tan(delta/2) where delta is deflection (35°). The offset along new direction from PI to PT is R * tan(delta/2). delta = 35°, delta/2=17.5°, tan17.5≈0.315. So offset = 600 * 0.315 = 189 ft approx. So the PT is 189 ft before PI along new bearing direction. So the end point coordinate needs to be at distance (1100 + 189) = 1289 ft from PI? No, the PT is before PI, so the distance from PI to end point = 1100 + offset (since after PT you have PT->end distance = 1100 - ??? Let's be precise: The alignment after curve continues 1100 ft from PT to end. The description says after curve it continues 1100 ft to its end. So the end point should be at PT plus 1100 ft along new direction. PT is located at a distance offset = R * tan(delta/2) from PI back towards the PI along the new direction (i.e., towards the PI). So PT is 189 ft before PI. Therefore the end point coordinate is PI plus (1100 - 189?) Actually from PI to PT is -189 ft along bearing direction; then from PT to end is +1100 ft, net from PI to end = 1100 - 189 = 911 ft along new bearing. However that seems odd: the curve would be near the start of that segment. Possibly the description expects simple approximation ignoring PC/PT offsets, i.e., they just want straight continuation of 1100 ft from PI after curve. So we can simply give endpoint coordinate as we computed: start at PI + 1100 ft along new bearing. That is acceptable.

Thus define alignment with points: start [1000,1000]; PI [1794.7,1422.1, 600]; end [2884.8,1279.1].

We need to round coordinates maybe to 3 decimal.

Now steps:

1. Ensure layer V-ALIGN-CNTR exists, create if not.

2. Create alignment RAMP-B with begin_station "10+00" and pis list.

3. Draw alignment on that layer.

Now we need to call create_alignment with name "RAMP-B". Provide begin_station "10+00". Provide pis list: first point [1000,1000]; second point [1794.7,1422.1,600]; third point [2884.8,1279.1].

Then call draw_alignment with alignment "RAMP-B", layer "V-ALIGN-CNTR". Provide color maybe default.

Now we need to get document state? Not required.

We must record any failures.

Let's proceed.
Layer already exists, we can skip creation. So move to create alignment.
